title: The Crane Wife
text:
A poor, lonely young man found a crane lying in the snow with an arrow through its wing. He pulled the arrow out, cleaned the wound and let the bird fly away.

Not long after, on a snowy night, a beautiful young woman knocked at his door, asking for shelter. She stayed, and before long they were married. They were very poor, so she offered to weave cloth for him to sell. She had only one condition: while she was weaving, he must never look into the room.

She shut herself in for days. When she came out, pale and thin, she carried a bolt of cloth so beautiful that it sold for a great price. The money ran out, and he asked her to weave again. She did, and grew thinner still. Encouraged by the money, or by neighbors who saw a chance to get rich, he asked a third time.

This time curiosity got the better of him. He slid the door open a crack and saw not his wife but a crane at the loom, plucking out its own feathers and weaving them into the cloth.

The crane saw him too. She came out, told him that she was the bird he had saved and that now that he had seen her true form she could not stay, then flew away and never came back.
lesson: Trust in a marriage rests on keeping promises, including the small ones about privacy. And asking a loved one to give more and more can use them up.
people: A poor man, his wife who is a crane
source: Japanese folktale (Tsuru Nyobo, The Crane Wife); a related tale is Tsuru no Ongaeshi
caveat: The tale exists in many regional versions, and in some the grateful crane comes to an old couple as a daughter rather than a wife.
